synopsis.why: Bowhead whales can live for more than 200 years and weigh over 80,000 kg, yet they are not especially prone to cancer. With that many cells dividing for that long, you would expect far more cancer, a puzzle known as Peto's paradox. If we knew how the whale protects its genome, we would learn something about why DNA damage builds up in people as we age, and about which repair systems are worth strengthening. This paper is one of the clearest tests so far of the idea that better DNA repair, rather than extra tumour-suppressor genes, can buy a long life.
synopsis.did: The team grew skin-type cells (fibroblasts) from bowhead whales and compared them with cells from humans and other mammals. First they counted how many cancer-causing genetic "hits" it took to turn the cells malignant. Then they measured how well the cells fixed double-strand breaks, the most dangerous kind of DNA damage, and how often new mutations appeared. When one protein, CIRBP, stood out as unusually abundant in the whale, they put the whale version into human cells and into fruit flies to see what it changed.
synopsis.found: Surprisingly, whale cells needed fewer cancer-causing hits than human cells to become malignant, so the whale is not protected by a harder-to-break cancer barrier. Instead, whale cells repaired double-strand breaks more often and more faithfully, and they built up mutations more slowly than cells of other mammals. CIRBP, a cold-inducible RNA-binding protein, was highly expressed in whale cells and tissues. The whale form of CIRBP boosted both main break-repair routes (non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination) in human cells, cut down micronuclei (small fragments of broken chromosome), protected broken DNA ends, and stimulated end joining in a test tube. Extra CIRBP extended lifespan in fruit flies and made them more resistant to radiation. The authors conclude that the whale keeps its genome intact by repairing damage well rather than by getting rid of damaged cells.
synopsis.limits: Most of the work was done on cultured cells and in fruit flies, not in living whales or people, and the fly lifespan result comes from overexpressing the protein. The abstract does not show that raising CIRBP would make humans live longer or lower cancer risk. Comparing species also leaves room for many other differences between whales and humans to matter.

A quick repair route that glues broken DNA ends back together, sometimes losing a few letters.
A more accurate repair route that copies the missing sequence from the matching chromosome.

synopsis.why: Some parts of the genome are short DNA motifs repeated many times in a row. synopsis.why: A double-strand break, where both strands of the DNA helix are cut, is one of the most dangerous things that can happen to a genome. They then blocked tubulin acetylation to see how nuclear shape, the movement of broken DNA and repair by homologous recombination changed, and in a separate step they removed the vimentin cage to see whether that reversed the effects. synopsis.why: Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, carry their own small genome, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). synopsis.why: DNA damage builds up as we age, and many researchers see it as one of the central drivers of aging rather than just a side effect. The most dangerous kind is the double-strand break, where both strands of the DNA helix are cut. If damage really pushes aging forward, then helping cells repair it better should slow aging down. They tested it in aged cells and in cells from patients with two genetic conditions marked by widespread DNA damage and early aging: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS), a rare disease of very fast aging in children, and Down syndrome (DS). They looked at how well cells repaired double-strand breaks, at the structure of the cell nucleus, and at patterns of gene activity. whyItMatters: A DNA polymerase best known in dividing cells turns out to help neurons keep their DNA in repair, and boosting it eased damage and Alzheimer's-related signs in lab neurons.

synopsis.why: Neurons are postmitotic: once mature, they stop dividing and have to last a lifetime. That means they cannot replace damaged DNA by copying it into new cells, so they rely on constant DNA repair. Many repair routes need a polymerase, an enzyme that fills in fresh DNA where damaged pieces were cut out. Which polymerases do this job in neurons is still poorly understood. synopsis.did: According to the abstract, the team studied DNA polymerase kappa (POLK), a so-called translesion synthesis polymerase that can copy across damaged DNA and has mostly been studied in dividing cells. They used primary mouse cortical neurons and human forebrain neurons made from induced pluripotent stem cells. They checked where POLK sits in the nucleus relative to newly made DNA and repair proteins, including a tagged form of PCNA (ubiquitinated PCNA) that marks repair activity. They then lowered POLK levels, and separately raised them, and measured DNA synthesis, signs of stress and senescence, inflammation, and stress signalling. They also tested neurons with a genetic background that raises Alzheimer's disease risk.
synopsis.found: POLK was found close to newly made DNA and to repair-associated proteins, including ubiquitinated PCNA. Lowering POLK reduced DNA synthesis in both mouse and human neurons. synopsis.limits: This is a preprint and has not yet been peer reviewed. This synopsis is based on the abstract only. synopsis.why: Age-related osteoporosis happens when the body makes too little new bone and the inner, spongy (trabecular) bone thins out. Bone-forming cells called osteoblasts decline in number and function with age, and more of them become senescent. Genome instability and ongoing DNA damage are thought to be part of this decline. This study looks at SIRT5, a mitochondrial enzyme that removes chemical tags called succinyl groups from proteins.
synopsis.did: According to the abstract, the researchers first combined public single-cell RNA sequencing data from mouse bone marrow to track age changes in the osteoblast lineage. They then studied naturally aged mice and mice lacking either Sirt5 or Prmt6 (another enzyme), measuring bone with micro-CT scans and tissue staining. They used RNA sequencing, proteomics that measure protein succinylation, a mapping method for R-loops (S9.6 CUT&Tag), and protein and imaging tests. synopsis.why: Epigenetic clocks estimate biological age from DNA methylation, mostly the mark called 5-methylcytosine (5mC). They are among the most promising measures of how fast someone is aging, yet nobody fully understands what drives the methylation changes they track. One overlooked piece is that 5mC can be chemically oxidised by TET enzymes into other forms, chiefly 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), as well as 5-formylcytosine and 5-carboxylcytosine. synopsis.did: This is a review article. According to the abstract, the authors gather current evidence on these oxidised forms of 5mC in mammalian aging, with most attention on 5hmC. synopsis.found: The review reports that aging is linked to changes in overall 5hmC levels and in its genome-wide pattern, and that these changes depend on context, such as tissue type. synopsis.limits: This synopsis is based on the abstract only, although the article is listed as open access. As a review, it summarises other studies and does not present new data; the abstract does not say how studies were chosen. The described changes are context-dependent, so general statements about 5hmC and aging may not hold in every tissue. 5hmC-based clocks are proposed here, not shown to work better than existing ones.

synopsis.why: The aging heart stiffens and scars (fibrosis), pumps less well, and loses some of its ability to repair itself, and this drives much of the illness and death from heart disease in older people. title: Concordance with the MIND diet is associated with lower subsequent epigenetic aging

whyItMatters: In 1,740 older Americans, eating closer to the brain-focused MIND diet went with slightly slower epigenetic aging three years later on three different clocks.

synopsis.why: Diet is one of the most commonly suggested ways to slow biological aging, but evidence that a specific eating pattern relates to later changes in aging markers is limited. The MIND diet (Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay) combines features of the Mediterranean and DASH diets with a focus on brain health. synopsis.did: According to the abstract, the researchers used the Health and Retirement Study, a large long-running study of older Americans. They linked diet information collected in 2013 to DNA methylation measured in 2016 in 1,740 participants. They scored how closely each person's diet matched MIND and related it to three epigenetic aging measures: PhenoAge acceleration, GrimAge acceleration and methylation Pace of Aging. They adjusted for other factors, corrected for multiple testing, and checked the results with additional adjustment for body-mass index, with weighting for how participants were selected, with a different causal estimation method (targeted maximum likelihood estimation), and with causal forests, a machine-learning method to look for subgroups who might benefit more.

title: Recurrent mitotic error and purifying selection shape chromosomal mosaicism across human tissues

openAccess.source: bioRxiv preprints are free to read (Crossref license metadata, fetched 2026-11-03: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

whyItMatters: Deep sequencing of 19 healthy tissues from 25 older donors maps where large chromosome errors pile up with age, and shows the body weeds most of them out.

synopsis.why: Every time a cell divides it has to copy and split its chromosomes perfectly. Sometimes it does not, and a daughter cell ends up missing a chromosome, carrying an extra one, or losing a large chunk of one. These large changes are called mosaic chromosomal alterations, because only some cells in the body carry them, like tiles in a mosaic. Scientists know a lot about them in cancer and in blood, where they are part of clonal hematopoiesis, the age-related expansion of mutated blood cell families. Much less is known about how common they are in healthy solid organs such as the heart, lung or glands, and how that changes as people age. Because genomic instability is considered one of the hallmarks of aging, a map of these errors across the body helps show where chromosome damage accumulates and whether the body tolerates it.
synopsis.did: According to the abstract, the team used very deep whole-genome sequencing (more than 200-fold coverage) produced by the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network, a large research consortium. The data covered 19 different tissues from 25 donors aged 42 to over 89, for a total of 722 tissue samples. They searched these samples for chromosome changes longer than one million DNA letters, for losses of the sex chromosomes (X and Y), and for copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, a change where a cell keeps the normal amount of DNA but both copies of a region come from the same parent.
synopsis.found: The researchers found 1,008 large mosaic changes on the non-sex chromosomes, and losses of the sex chromosomes turned up everywhere. Unexpectedly, loss of the Y chromosome in men was highest in the lung, adrenal gland and heart, reaching roughly 5 to 10 percent of cells in elderly donors. Those same tissues tended to show more X loss in women, which the authors read as a gradient in how often cell division goes wrong from tissue to tissue. Changes in whole chromosome number showed tissue-specific patterns suggesting that the body usually selects against cells carrying them. The adrenal gland was an exception, with low levels of such errors almost everywhere. The testis rarely had extra or missing chromosomes, but it often showed copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, hinting at more frequent swapping between paired chromosomes in sperm stem cells. Repeated X losses in women's tissues favoured one parental copy over the other, which the authors explain through a mix of genetic and epigenetic effects. Overall, they conclude that the chromosome landscape of aging tissues is shaped by genetics and recurring errors, and that most of these errors are kept in check by purifying selection, the removal of less fit cells.
synopsis.limits: This is a preprint, so it has not yet been checked by independent peer reviewers, and the findings could change. The study included 25 donors, which is a small number of people even though many tissues were sampled from each, and all donors were middle-aged or older, so it cannot show directly how these changes build up from youth. The abstract describes patterns and the authors' interpretation of selection; it does not report effects on health or disease. This synopsis was written from the abstract only.

whyItMatters: In mouse skin, losing the antioxidant switch NRF2 made DNA mutations pile up faster with age, while barely changing mutations from a burst of UV light.

synopsis.why: Our cells constantly make reactive oxygen species, chemically aggressive molecules that are a by-product of normal metabolism and are also produced by outside stresses such as ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun. These molecules can damage DNA, and damaged DNA can turn into permanent mutations. The slow build-up of mutations in body tissues is thought to contribute to aging and to cancer. NRF2 is a master switch protein that turns on many of the cell's antioxidant defences. A natural question is how much NRF2 actually protects DNA, and whether that protection matters more against a sudden hit like sunburn or against the quiet, lifelong stress of normal metabolism.
synopsis.did: According to the abstract, the researchers studied mice that lack the Nrf2 gene and compared them with normal mice. The mice carried a bacterial gene called lacZ as a mutation reporter: because this gene sits in the mouse DNA but does nothing for the animal, scientists can recover it and count and characterise the mutations it has picked up. The team looked at the epidermis, the outer layer of the skin, in two situations: after acute exposures to UVB light, and over the natural course of aging. They compared how many mutations appeared, what kinds of mutations they were, and where they fell within the reporter gene.
synopsis.found: After acute UVB exposure, the abstract reports no significant differences between Nrf2-deficient and normal mice in how many mutations appeared, in the types of mutations, or in their positions in the reporter gene. They saw little sign that reactive oxygen species drove the DNA damage after the acute exposure. In contrast, the age-related build-up of mutations was significantly higher in skin lacking Nrf2 than in normal skin. The authors conclude that NRF2 protects the skin mainly by helping tissue recover after acute UV damage and, more importantly, by limiting the DNA-damaging effects of the body's own oxidants during chronic aging.
synopsis.limits: The study was done in mice, in one tissue (the outer skin), and it uses an artificial bacterial reporter gene to count mutations, which may not behave exactly like the body's own genes. The abstract does not give the ages of the mice, the size of the differences or the number of animals, so it is hard to judge how large the effect is. title: PARP-CD38-Driven NAD+ Loss in Immune Aging: An Emerging Mechanistic Framework
whyItMatters: A review proposing how the DNA-repair enzyme PARP and the enzyme CD38 together drain the cell fuel NAD+ in aging immune cells, and why that matters for anti-aging drugs.

synopsis.why: As the immune system ages it becomes both weaker and more inflamed, a state often called inflammaging. One idea links this to NAD+, a molecule cells need for energy and for many repair jobs. A family of enzymes called PARPs uses up NAD+ when they respond to DNA damage, especially PARP1, the main enzyme that flags broken DNA for repair. Another enzyme, CD38, also breaks down NAD+ and becomes more common in inflamed, aged tissues. NAD+ boosting supplements and PARP-blocking drugs are both being explored, so understanding how DNA-damage responses, NAD+ and immune aging fit together matters for anyone weighing these approaches.
synopsis.did: This is a review article, so the authors did not run new experiments. According to the abstract, they gathered existing research and proposed a framework they call a context-dependent PARP-CD38-NAD+-inflammaging hierarchy. They looked beyond PARP1 at other members of the family and at how NAD+ is kept in separate pools inside the cell, each with its own enzymes for making and moving it.
synopsis.found: The authors note that PARP1 accounts for about 85 to 90 percent of PARP activity in the nucleus and is the main consumer of NAD+ during acute DNA damage, while CD38 is the main NAD+-destroying enzyme and rises in inflamed, aged tissue. They point out that NAD+ is held in distinct compartments, such as the cytosol and the mitochondria, with different regulators. They highlight recent human data that challenge the idea that NAD+ declines everywhere with age: one study found that an 85 percent drop in muscle NAD+ did not impair function, and whole-blood NAD+ did not change with age. From this they argue that NAD+ decline is specific to tissues and compartments, and that blood NAD+ is not a reliable marker. They list other PARPs tied to aging of particular tissues in models, including PARP2 in mouse heart muscle cells, PARP3 in the gut, PARP16 in blood vessels and PARP9 and PARP14 in Alzheimer's models, while noting their roles in human immune aging are not yet measured. PARP inhibitors and NAD+ precursors show promise, they write, but carry risks including genomic instability, blood-cell toxicity, promoting senescence and inconsistent benefit.

whyItMatters: A direct test of the idea that DNA damage ages cells by erasing their epigenetic identity finds that repeated cell division, not radiation damage, wears that identity down in human skin cells.

synopsis.why: Every cell in the body carries the same DNA, but a skin cell and a liver cell use it differently. Part of what keeps each cell type distinct is DNA methylation, small chemical tags on DNA that help set which genes stay on or off. One influential theory of aging says that DNA damage, and the repair work it triggers, slowly scrambles these tags so that cells lose the information that tells them what they are. If that were true, protecting DNA would also protect cell identity. This preprint sets out to test that specific proposed cause directly, while making clear it is not testing the broader idea that aging involves some loss of epigenetic information.
synopsis.did: According to the abstract, the team built a panel of 9,150 CpG sites (places in DNA that can carry a methylation tag) where human skin fibroblasts differ most from twenty other primary cell types, since those are the sites where identity should be easiest to measure. They noticed that many of these sites mainly record how much a cell has divided, so they separated that layer from true identity marks. They then scored each treatment as the share of identity information lost beyond matched background sites. In 24 matched fibroblast cultures they compared replicative exhaustion (cells dividing until they stop), activation of the cancer gene RAS, a senescence-inducing dose of X-rays, and senescence caused by the chemotherapy drug doxorubicin.
synopsis.found: Most of the panel behaved as a record of proliferation rather than identity, matching the gradual loss of methylation in late-replicating DNA that builds up when cells are grown in culture. Replicative exhaustion cost 24.3 percent of the identity information and RAS activation cost 5.4 percent. A senescence-inducing dose of X-rays cost nothing, at minus 0.5 percent, with identity sites if anything moving slightly further away from other cell types. The authors say their design could have detected a loss as small as 0.4 percent, so they treat this as a real negative result rather than a lack of power. Senescence induced by doxorubicin or by irradiation did not shift the panel either, and cells that kept dividing after irradiation moved further from other cell types rather than collapsing toward them. Their conclusion is that, in human fibroblasts, loss of identity information follows prolonged division, not acute DNA damage.
synopsis.limits: This is a preprint and has not yet been through peer review. The work uses one cell type, skin fibroblasts, grown in the lab, and tests acute damage from X-rays and a drug rather than the slow, lifelong damage that happens in a living body, so it may not settle what happens in aging tissues. title: TERRA: an induced responder to telomere dysfunction

openAccess.source: Crossref license metadata, fetched 2026-11-04: CC BY 4.0

whyItMatters: A review arguing that TERRA, an RNA made at chromosome tips, works like a dial that first tries to fix damaged telomeres and, if that fails, pushes the cell into senescence.

synopsis.why: Telomeres are protective caps of repeated DNA at the ends of our chromosomes. They shorten as cells divide and can be damaged, and short or damaged telomeres are one of the recognised hallmarks of aging because they can stop cells dividing or make them inflammatory. Telomeres are not silent: they are copied into an RNA called TERRA, short for telomeric repeat-containing RNA. For years TERRA was seen as a permanent, built-in part of telomeres. Understanding what it really does could explain how cells decide between repairing a worn-out chromosome end and retiring the cell, a decision that matters for both aging and cancer.
synopsis.did: This is a review and perspective article, so the authors did not run new experiments. According to the abstract, they bring together experimental evidence from yeasts and mammals on when TERRA is made, what it interacts with, and what happens to cells when its levels change. They then propose a model for TERRA's role.
synopsis.found: The authors argue that TERRA is not a constant fixture but a stress signal made specifically at telomeres that are not working properly. Its levels change as telomeres shorten or become damaged, and it helps call in the right repair route through contacts with shelterin (the protein complex that protects telomeres), with chromatin regulators and with DNA repair factors. It also does this through the controlled formation of R-loops, structures where the RNA pairs with the DNA. In cells without telomerase, the enzyme that can lengthen telomeres, a brief rise in TERRA and R-loops encourages telomeres to be lengthened by copying from another DNA template. In cells with telomerase, TERRA seems to steer the enzyme toward the shortest telomeres. When damage is not resolved, however, lasting TERRA production and persistent R-loops drive cells toward senescence, inflammatory signalling and cell death. The authors propose that TERRA acts as a molecular rheostat, or dial: short, well-placed bursts restore the chromosome end, while long-term build-up removes damaged cells from the dividing pool.
synopsis.limits: As a review, this proposes a model rather than proving it, and the authors themselves say the key next step is to define how cells set these switch points. Much of the underlying evidence comes from yeast and cultured cells, so how the model applies to aging human tissues is still open. This synopsis was written from the abstract only, although the full review is free to read.

title: Epigenetic aging during the COVID-19 pandemic: A prospective longitudinal study with prepandemic baseline data in children, adolescents, and adults
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

openAccess.source: Crossref license metadata, fetched 2026-11-04: CC BY 4.0

whyItMatters: Saliva DNA from about 1,000 German children, teens and young adults, collected before and during the pandemic, showed epigenetic clocks ticking faster, especially in teens who felt more burdened.

synopsis.why: Long-term psychological stress is a known risk factor for diseases that come with aging. Epigenetic clocks, tools that estimate biological age from patterns of DNA methylation tags, are increasingly used as early warning signs of that risk. The COVID-19 pandemic, with lockdowns, school closures and worry, was a stress felt by whole populations at once. Most studies of stress and epigenetic aging measure people only after the fact, so they cannot say what changed. A study with samples taken just before the pandemic offers a rare chance to see whether biological aging measures actually shifted, and who was most affected.
synopsis.did: According to the abstract, the researchers used prospective longitudinal data from 1,028 people in Germany: 359 children (average age 9.5), 385 adolescents (average 15.5) and 284 adults (average 24.3). Saliva for DNA was collected before the first lockdown measures in March 2020 and again after the second phase of measures in 2021. They applied four epigenetic clocks, DunedinPACE, GrimAge2, Horvath and PedBE, and tested whether any changes were linked to objective pandemic stressors, to how burdened people felt, and to existing risk factors for poorer physical and mental health.
synopsis.found: Epigenetic age acceleration rose significantly on the PedBE and GrimAge2 clocks, and the pace of aging measured by DunedinPACE also increased, across all three age groups. These changes were linked to physical health before the pandemic and to parents' socioeconomic status, but not to objective pandemic stressors. In adolescents, a higher perceived burden from the pandemic went along with a larger increase in pace of aging. The authors conclude that existing risk factors for poorer health were accompanied by measurable increases in epigenetic aging during the pandemic, and that adolescence may be a particularly sensitive period for its psychological burden.
synopsis.limits: The study has no comparison group that lived through the same period without a pandemic, so it cannot fully separate pandemic effects from normal changes over a year of growth and development, which matter a lot in children and teens. Clocks were measured in saliva, and epigenetic clocks are estimates whose link to later disease in young people is not yet proven. The abstract reports statistical effect sizes but not what they mean in years of biological age. This synopsis was written from the abstract only, although the full paper is free to read.

title: The divergent 3D genome landscapes of aging and neurodegenerative mouse models

openAccess.source: Europe PMC reports subscription required; Crossref lists no open license (checked 2026-11-05)

whyItMatters: Hi-C maps of mouse cortical neurons suggest normal aging softens 3D genome organization into a primed state, while neurodegeneration models add DNA-damage-linked collapse of loops and compartments.

synopsis.why: Neurons keep the same DNA for a lifetime, so how that DNA is folded in three dimensions matters for which genes stay on and for keeping the genome stable. That folding slowly frays with age and is more badly disrupted in neurodegenerative disease, but it has been unclear whether aging and disease follow the same early path or branch apart. If aging only primes the nucleus and disease adds a further hit such as DNA damage, that would change how we read chromatin maps from old brains and where we look for interventions.
synopsis.did: According to the abstract, the authors ran Hi-C, a method that maps which stretches of DNA sit near each other in the nucleus, on cortical neurons from adult mice, aged mice, and mice with a brain-specific knockout of SIRT6. They compared those maps with previously published Hi-C data from a CK-p25 Alzheimer's disease model that had been split by levels of γH2AX, a mark of DNA damage. They looked at contacts between chromosomes, A/B compartments (active versus quieter genome neighborhoods), topologically associating domains (TADs), architectural loops, and enhancer-promoter loops.
synopsis.found: All of the models shared early features: weaker contacts between chromosomes in larger nuclei, shifts of regions from the active A compartment toward the quieter B compartment, and loss of architectural loops. Aged neurons still kept TAD structure, short-range contacts, and enhancer-promoter loops relatively intact. The pathological models instead showed weaker TAD prominence, shorter loops, and messy mixing of A and B compartments, and those deeper changes tracked with higher DNA damage. The authors interpret ordinary aging as a primed state in which chromatin control has started to erode, while extra stress such as DNA damage is linked to the fuller breakdown seen in neurodegeneration.
synopsis.limits: This synopsis was written from the abstract only; the paper is not open access. The work is in mouse cortical neurons and a specific Alzheimer's model, so how far it generalizes to human aging brains is open. The comparison mixes new Hi-C with previously published disease maps, and correlation with γH2AX does not by itself prove that DNA damage causes the structural collapse.

title: Evolution of the human methylome in blood from embryo to ageing and cancer

openAccess.source: Crossref license metadata, fetched 2026-11-05: CC BY 4.0

whyItMatters: Single-cell blood lineages show that heritable DNA methylation changes far outpace mutations across life, and that epigenetic clocks largely report which clones dominate blood rather than calendar age.

synopsis.why: DNA methylation tags help lock in what a cell is, and they are copied when the cell divides. Those tags also drift with age and shift in cancer, but until now it was hard to watch how the methylome evolves inside single human blood lineages over a lifetime. Knowing whether age-related methylation is mostly developmental leftover, clone expansion, or new damage would change how we read epigenetic clocks and clonal hematopoiesis.
synopsis.did: According to the abstract, the team matched whole-methylome and whole-genome sequencing from 1,183 single-cell-derived haematopoietic colonies from 13 people. The donors spanned 17 weeks after conception to 77 years of age, healthy blood formation to malignancy, and included monozygotic twins. That design let them reconstruct when methylation states arose, how often they changed relative to DNA letter mutations, and how those states behaved in clonal expansions and blood cancers.
synopsis.found: Heritable methylation change ran about six orders of magnitude faster than single-base DNA mutations before birth and about four orders faster afterward, often flipping whole stretches of CpG sites at once. Each blood cell already carried about 300,000 somatic methylation changes before birth, including more than 3,000 large segments that then stayed stable for decades. The authors call these large segments embryonic epialleles: places where lineages of the same cell type in one person keep different heritable methylation states. They found about 250,000 such segments across the cohort, many shared between people, and used the mosaic to time X-chromosome inactivation to the first few divisions of life. Epigenetic age, they argue, mainly reports the division history of whichever clones currently dominate the blood, not the person's calendar age. In clonal expansions and blood cancer, many methylation differences versus background were embryonic states the founder cell already carried; expansions nonetheless converged on Polycomb-associated regulatory regions, usually gaining methylation but losing it when DNMT3A was mutated. A few changes at known cancer genes, including CDKN2B, ABL1 in BCR::ABL1 disease, and CACNA1D, arose only inside expansions and looked like epigenetic drivers. Because methylation can change which transcript a gene makes or whether it is expressed, the authors cast methylation mosaicism as another widespread substrate for Darwinian evolution inside the body.
synopsis.limits: This is a preprint and has not yet been through peer review. The synopsis was written from the abstract only, although the preprint is free to read. The work is in blood-forming cells, so tissue-specific aging elsewhere is not mapped here. Colony-based sequencing captures heritable states that survive cloning in culture and may miss some unstable marks.

title: Cross-species epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity: Insights from Jonathan the Giant Tortoise and human centenarians

openAccess.source: bioRxiv preprints are free to read (Crossref license metadata, fetched 2026-11-05: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

whyItMatters: A comparative DNA-methylation analysis finds shared entropy patterns between a 194-year-old giant tortoise and human supercentenarians, enriched at telomere-related genes.

synopsis.why: Some animals and some people live far longer than their peers, and DNA methylation patterns are one place those differences might show up. If the epigenomic footprints of extreme longevity look alike in species that last branched apart hundreds of millions of years ago, that would point to conserved aging biology rather than a quirk of one tissue or one lineage. Jonathan, a giant tortoise about 194 years old, and human supercentenarians offer a rare chance to ask that question with existing methylation data.
synopsis.did: According to the abstract, this is a comparative reanalysis rather than a new animal experiment. The authors set findings from a published epigenomic study of Jonathan, based on buccal scrape and saliva samples, beside publicly available DNA methylation data from exceptionally long-lived humans measured in blood mononuclear cells. They compared global methylation entropy and promoter-level entropy patterns across age groups and asked which biological pathways the distinctive human genes pointed to.
synopsis.found: People aged 110 and older showed significantly higher global methylation entropy than people aged 60 to 82. Twelve candidate genes had a distinctive promoter methylation entropy shape, lower at the youngest and oldest ages than in middle age. Those genes were enriched for telomere-related processes, linking the epigenomic pattern to a pathway already central in aging biology. The authors say the human pattern lines up with what had been reported in Jonathan, and they present that correspondence as a source of testable hypotheses about longevity signatures that might be conserved across species and not only tissue-specific.
synopsis.limits: This is a preprint and has not yet been through peer review. It reuses published datasets from different tissues (mouth in the tortoise, blood in humans), so shared patterns could still partly reflect tissue or technical differences. Entropy summaries are one way to compress methylation data and may miss other relevant signals. This synopsis was written from the abstract only, although the full preprint is free to read.
